<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Mustafa Omer Gul
</span><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_note ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Work done during an internship at Microsoft Research.</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Philippe Laban
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Cornell University  Microsoft Research<span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">momergul@cs.cornell.edu ; {plaban,tanyagoyal,jenneville}@microsoft.com</span>
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Tanya Goyal
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Cornell University  Microsoft Research<span id="id3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">momergul@cs.cornell.edu ; {plaban,tanyagoyal,jenneville}@microsoft.com</span>
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jennifer Neville
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Cornell University  Microsoft Research<span id="id4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">momergul@cs.cornell.edu ; {plaban,tanyagoyal,jenneville}@microsoft.com</span>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Users increasingly rely on AI systems for extended, multi-turn tasks, yet evidence indicates that LLM-based system performance degrades over prolonged interaction. To evaluate and improve AI assistants in such settings, we need user simulators that faithfully follow complex user intents while exhibiting realistic conversational behavior. Existing approaches manifest a trade-off: prompted assistants can follow complex user intents but lack behavioral fidelity, while specialized user simulators better approximate conversational behavior but struggle to remain faithful to complex intents. In this paper, we propose a reinforcement learning (RL) recipe that jointly rewards task intent adherence and behavioral naturalness. A crucial contribution of the method is operationalizing naturalness with a lightweight discriminator trained in an alternating, adversarial loop with the user simulator. We release the resulting model, <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">UserLM-2.0</span>, which produces valid simulated conversations (i.e., meeting both task-faithfulness and naturalness criteria) 46.2% of the time, over three times the rate of the strongest prior user simulator (14.1%).</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">
<tr id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:24.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span></td></tr>
</table>
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S0.F1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><a href="https://huggingface.co/microsoft/UserLM-2.0" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href ltx_font_typewriter"><span class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:2.6pt;"><img src="2610.31512v1/figures/huggingface.png" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:15/15;" width="15" height="15" alt="Refer to caption"></span> <span class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">microsoft/UserLM-2.0</span></a></p></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.31512v1/teaser3.svg" id="S0.F1.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/354;" width="548" height="354"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>We train and release UserLM-2.0, a user simulator for User-AI interaction optimized via RL to precisely enact user intents while exhibiting natural conversational behavior. In comparison, assistants such as GPT-5.6-Sol follow intents, but sound unnatural, while SFT-trained simulators like UserLM-8B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naous et al., 2026</a>)</cite> generate natural, but meandering conversations.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Users increasingly expect AI assistants and agents to help them accomplish complex tasks through sustained, multi-turn interaction, rather than provide isolated answers to individual queries <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Handa et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chatterji et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Yet prior work has shown that current LLM-based systems severely degrade in performance in such interactive settings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Laban et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tack et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Understanding and addressing this gap requires evaluations that capture how real users communicate their goals and respond to assistants over multiple turns <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. A crucial component of interactive benchmarks is a <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">user simulator</span>, which takes as input a high-level <span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">task intent</span> (such as the one shown in Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) and generates plausible user utterances through iterative interaction with an assistant <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We focus on two essential properties of user simulators: task fidelity and behavioral naturalness. Task fidelity requires the simulator to convey the information specified in the task intent over the course of the conversation, without omitting or contradicting the specification. Behavioral naturalness requires the simulator to resemble real users in both how it phrases individual messages and how it conducts the interaction across turns. A simulator that omits task requirements can make assistant models appear to fail when the simulator is at fault, making benchmarking unreliable <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mehri et al., 2026c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, whereas a simulator that does not adequately capture the interactive behavior of real users may yield conclusions that do not transfer to real interactions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Seshadri et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We show experimentally that current approaches favor one requirement at the expense of the other. Prompting LLM assistants to act as users is the most common method for simulating users <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. While prompted assistants can stay on task, they lack behavioral naturalness <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naous et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mehri et al., 2026a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. This is illustrated in the example in Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, where GPT-5.6-Sol (a strong assistant LLM) accurately enacts the task intent but expresses it through unusually polished and exhaustive messages, unlike the conversational patterns in real user-AI exchanges.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">An alternative is to train user simulators by “flipping the dialogue”: supervised finetuning an LLM on user utterances from a corpus of user-assistant interactions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naous et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suh et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. As reported in prior work, such finetuned user simulators exhibit realistic interaction behavior but often struggle to precisely enact the task intent they are given <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naous et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. In the example in Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the SFT-trained UserLM-8B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naous et al., 2026</a>)</cite> ends the conversation prematurely, before conveying all of the specified task requirements to the assistant.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a post-training recipe that improves task fidelity while preserving behavioral naturalness in user simulators. We first finetune an LLM on user turns from a corpus of user-assistant interactions, then post-train it using multi-turn reinforcement learning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Our RL training objective jointly rewards task fidelity and behavioral naturalness. Rewards related to task fidelity use LLM-based judges <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, for example by evaluating the extent to which a simulated conversation has conveyed the information specified in the task intent. We find that LLM-as-a-judge for behavioral naturalness fails to reliably encourage realistic user behavior. Instead, drawing on adversarial training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goodfellow et al., 2014b</a>)</cite> and its application to dialogue generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, we propose a discriminator-based reward for behavioral naturalness. Specifically, we continually retrain a discriminator to distinguish real user conversations from conversations generated by the user simulator being trained. This choice defines the naturalness reward in terms of how indistinguishable a given simulated conversation is from real user conversations. We update the discriminator as the simulator evolves to keep the naturalness reward responsive to its changing outputs and reduce opportunities to exploit a fixed evaluator <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">We train, evaluate, and release the resulting artifact, UserLM-2.0. Among the simulators we evaluated, UserLM-2.0 lies on the Pareto frontier for task fidelity and behavioral naturalness. We count a simulated conversation as valid if it adheres to our quality and termination criteria, achieves at least 80% coverage of the task intent <span id="S1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">and</span> passes our naturalness criterion, assessed using three discriminators including Pangram <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Glickenhaus et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. By this definition, UserLM-2.0 yields valid conversations for 46.2% of task intents, more than three times the 14.1% rate of the strongest prior user simulator (SFTUser-14B). This gap grows even further to a factor of 12 at higher task complexities, highlighting the effectiveness of our method.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Method</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our goal is to train a user simulator that takes a high-level task intent as input, and simulates realistic user utterances in a multi-turn user-assistant conversation. As previously discussed, a good user simulator must (1) generate natural utterances, and (2) obey the task intents closely.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Problem Definition</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each conversation is a multi-turn interaction where a user simulator <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>U</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U</annotation></semantics></math> interacts with an assistant model <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> to satisfy an input intent <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>. This intent <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> captures the high-level goal of the user without detailing behavior on a turn-by-turn basis. Given <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>, we sample conversations
<math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=(c,u_{1},a_{1},\ldots,u_{n-1},a_{n-1},u_{n})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=(c,u_{1},a_{1},\ldots,u_{n-1},a_{n-1},u_{n})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> represent the sampled <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th user and assistant utterances respectively. A conversation terminates either when the maximum number of user turns <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> is reached or when the user outputs an <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;|endconversation|&gt;</span> tag.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naous et al., 2026</a>)</cite> trains user simulators via SFT on a large corpus of user-assistant interactions.
These exhibit the desired naturalness behavior, but are extremely poor at faithfully enacting task intents.
We propose treating such SFT models as initializations rather than the final user simulator. We train our own SFT model, UserLM-2.0-SFT, and design an RL-based post-training pipeline that improves its task fidelity without sacrificing naturalness.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We perform multi-turn reinforcement learning using the GRPO algorithm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Our reward balances the above two goals of user simulation, task fidelity and behavioral naturalness.
Although these are orthogonal, models can easily reward hack one at the cost of the other, such as by unnaturally including all information in the first utterance for perfect task coverage. The combined reward composition safeguards against such behaviors.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Reward Design For Reinforcement Learning</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first describe the individual reward components and then our formula for combining them:</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Naturalness:</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The naturalness reward should score how closely the user utterances of simulated conversation resemble the way real users interact with AI assistants in a target corpus.
Let <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{disc}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>disc</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{disc}}</annotation></semantics></math> be a discriminator that can distinguish between real and simulated user utterances. Our naturalness reward measures how well the user simulator fools such a discriminator based on <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{disc}}(y=\text{real}\mid\hat{u_{1}}...\hat{u_{k}},c)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>disc</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>real</mtext></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{disc}}(y=\text{real}\mid\hat{u_{1}}...\hat{u_{k}},c)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{u_{1}}...\hat{u_{k}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{u_{1}}...\hat{u_{k}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the multi-turn output from the user simulator and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> is the associated task intent. For training, we set our naturalness reward to be binary; it is <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> if this discriminator score is above a threshold (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math> in our experiments) and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> otherwise.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Broadly, we have two options for discriminators: LLM judges or specially trained discriminators. LLM judges are ill-suited for this task. Naturalness captures multiple implicit dimensions such as the surface-form of the utterance, pace of the conversation, coherence of follow-up utterances, etc., all of which might be impossible to extract from the target corpus and enumerate as instructions.
In fact, prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Russell et al., 2025</a>)</cite> has shown that prompted LLM judges are ineffective at distinguishing between real user and AI text.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
                
                
                
              Note that AI detection of assistant turns is an analogous task to user naturalness. There, the goal is to score the “naturalness” of AI assistants’ text to distinguish it from human-written text. We highlight that the best AI detectors in industry use trained discriminators instead of LLM judges <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Glickenhaus et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.</span></span></span> In our work, we train lightweight discriminators on top of ModernBert-Large <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Warner et al., 2025</a>)</cite> to distinguish between real and simulated user utterances. This allows us to both limit the costs and latency during RL and specialize to the user behaviors in the target corpus. We include ablations to empirically demonstrate the issues with using LLM judges and static discriminators in Section <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Reward Design Alternatives ‣ 4 Results and Analysis ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Coverage:</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This reward component quantifies how completely the user simulator follows a task intent. We define coverage as the proportion of the sub-goals of the task intent that are included in the user utterances generated by the simulator. This is instantiated with an LLM judge.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We highlight that coverage can be an easy metric to reward hack for user simulators. For example, given a detailed task intent with fully specified sub-goals, a user simulator can maximize coverage by simply paraphrasing the sub-goals. This is not ideal as it disincentivizes diverse simulations for the same task intent. Therefore, we introduce an information asymmetry between the task intent provided to the user simulator as input (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>) and the one used to compute the coverage reward by the LLM judge (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>), where <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> is a more abstract version of the fully-specified task intent <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>. This ensures the model receives poor coverage when simply paraphrasing, and encourages exploring more diverse behaviors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to coverage, we include two other reward components for task fidelity. These target proper formatting of the user utterances and elimination of trivial failure modes of the SFT models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Quality:</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our quality reward is a binary score that assesses the baseline quality of a simulated conversation. It targets three common error modes of the SFT models: (1) verbatim repetition of task intent, (2) verbatim repetition of past user turns, and (3) switching roles from user to assistant mid-output. We first check the initial two conditions programmatically and otherwise use an LLM judge. A simulated conversation is given a reward <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> if all three conditions are met, and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> otherwise.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Termination:</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The goal of the termination reward is to ensure that user simulators properly terminate conversations when all sub-goals in <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> are met and penalize early termination. We give a positive reward <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> for including the termination tag <span id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;|endconversation|&gt;</span> in the last utterance if all sub-goals have been met in the earlier utterances and a negative reward <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> if the conversation is terminated without satisfying all sub-goals. Note that this ties the termination reward to coverage. In some cases, the user simulator fails to terminate the conversation at all, i.e. does not generate the <span id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;|endconversation|&gt;</span> tag; in these cases, we give it a <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> termination reward.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Final Reward:</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We combine all four reward components into a overall reward score for a simulated conversation using the following formula:
<math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\text{overall}}=r_{\text{quality}}\cdot\left(r_{\text{coverage}}+r_{\text{naturalness}}+r_{\text{termination}}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>overall</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>quality</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>coverage</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>naturalness</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>termination</mtext></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\text{overall}}=r_{\text{quality}}\cdot\left(r_{\text{coverage}}+r_{\text{naturalness}}+r_{\text{termination}}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>. Note that the overall reward is <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> if the quality reward is <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>. Therefore, the basic quality checks serve as a necessary condition for any successful simulation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>GAN-Style Training with Dynamic Discriminators</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">One limitation of trained naturalness discriminators, especially lightweight ones with fewer parameters, is that a larger user simulator trained against it will quickly learn to reward hack. It will quickly converge on a narrow set of behaviors that reliably fools the specific discriminator but does not learn broader behavioral naturalness. Our initial experiments validated this intuition – user simulators trained against a static discriminator maximized the naturalness reward within 75 steps by greatly increasing average utterance length while reducing conversation turns.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To address this, we propose a GAN-style training recipe that periodically re-trains the discriminator every k steps. This improves discriminator quality by exposing it to synthetic conversations with distinct behavioral patterns and further helps detect and discourage reward hacking behavior.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Experimental Setup</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Dataset Construction</h3>

<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Dataset Processing.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We run our experiments on the non-toxic subset of WildChat-4.8M <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
We build on top of the dataset processing scheme of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naous et al. (2026)</a></cite>, additionally removing interactions with only one user turn as our goal is to simulate multi-turn interactions. This reduces the WildChat-4.8M dataset size from 3,199,860 to 199,249 interactions.
We also follow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naous et al. (2026)</a></cite> in how we construct train, validation and test sets.
We hold out 10,000 and 1,000 conversations from the train and validation set for RL training, 3,200 and 1,000 conversations from the train and validation set for discriminator training, and use the rest for SFT. Refer to Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Dataset Construction ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> for more details on dataset construction.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Intent and Subgoal Extraction.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We need to extract both intents (given as input for simulation) and fine-grained sub-goals (used for LLM-based coverage reward). We use Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> to extract intents for all 199,249 conversations. For sub-goals, we few-shot prompt the best available GPT models without reasoning. Details are in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Dataset Construction ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Test dataset.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report all results on a 2000 intent test set, constructed such that the number of intents per sub-goal count (ranging from 1 to 7) is balanced. For each user simulator, we sample four conversations per intent
with Qwen3.5-9B as the assistant.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Training Details</h3>

<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">User Simulator Training.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use Llama3.1-8B-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grattafiori et al., 2024</a>)</cite> as the backbone for UserLM-2.0. We replicate the SFT training of  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naous et al. (2026)</a></cite> and select the checkpoint with the best validation loss for subsequent RL. This checkpoint is UserLM-2.0-SFT. For RL, we simulate conversations with a maximum turn count of <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=5</annotation></semantics></math>, and use Qwen3.5-9B without reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team, 2026</a>)</cite> as the assistant model. We set <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=0.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=0.2</annotation></semantics></math> for the termination reward, batch size to <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>64</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64</annotation></semantics></math>, group size to <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math> and KL hyperparameter <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.001</annotation></semantics></math>. We measure model performance on the validation set every <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>25</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">25</annotation></semantics></math> steps for checkpoint selection. See Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Training Details ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> for further training details.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Naturalness Discriminator Training.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use the 395M ModernBERT-Large <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Warner et al., 2025</a>)</cite> as the discriminator. For each task intent, we sample one simulated conversation (using the user and assistant models) and one real conversation (from the ground truth dataset).<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
                
                
                
              We use only the user turns for discrimination, as we found including assistant turns made simulated conversations perfectly discriminable due to stylistic differences between assistants.</span></span></span> This ensures that our dataset is always balanced. We re-train our discriminator every <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>25</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">25</annotation></semantics></math> steps of RL training. At each iteration, half of our training dataset consists of conversations based on task intents from the most recent <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>25</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">25</annotation></semantics></math> RL steps, while the other half is sampled uniformly from the remaining training history. We train for five epochs and pick the checkpoint achieving the best validation accuracy. Refer to Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Discriminator Training Details ‣ Appendix B Training Details ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a> for exact hyperparameters and training details.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Baselines</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare UserLM-2.0  against two categories of models: assistant LLMs prompted to behave like users, and specialized finetuned user simulators, as well as held out reference users.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Finetuned Models.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare against USP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, UserLM-8B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naous et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, UserLM-2.0-SFT (our SFT initialization), SFTUser-14B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suh et al., 2026</a>)</cite> and HumanLM-Opinion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. UserLM-8B and SFTUser-14B are trained on WildChat-1M <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> via SFT but differ in their backbone initialization. USP is also SFT-trained but on a subset of 94,874 LMSys-Chat conversations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. HumanLM is trained via RL to align with latent states such as user goals, opinions or emotional valence.
We use the HumanLM-Opinion checkpoint as other HumanLM checkpoints have not been released. For USP and HumanLM-Opinion, we include the input intent and termination instructions in system prompts (details in Appendix <a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 Finetuned Baseline Inference Prompts ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Details ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Prompted assistant LLMs.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use a range of small and large, open- and closed-source models. Specifically, we evaluate: Llama3.1-8B-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grattafiori et al., 2024</a>)</cite> (Llama-3.1-8B in the tables), Qwen3.5-9B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team, 2026</a>)</cite>, GPT-5.6-Luna, GPT-5.6-Sol <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2026</a>)</cite>, DeepSeek-V4-Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2026</a>)</cite> and Kimi-K2.6 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moonshot AI, 2026</a>)</cite>. We follow the prompting strategy of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naous et al. (2026)</a></cite>, with prompts and inference details in Appendix <a href="#A3.SS2" title="C.2 Assistant Baseline Inference Prompts ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Details ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Evaluation Metrics</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate all simulators on a common set of 2,000 test task intents. For each task intent, we simulate four independent conversations and compute three evaluation metrics that assess task fidelity and three metrics that assess naturalness. Finally, we define a compound metric that assesses the overall <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">validity</span> of each simulated conversation.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Task Fidelity Metrics.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We assess each generated conversation by reusing the Terminated, Quality, and Coverage as defined in Section <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Reward Design For Reinforcement Learning ‣ 2 Method ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>. In short, Terminated is the percentage of conversations with an explicit <span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;|endconversation|&gt;</span> present. The Quality metric is a binary check for three undesirable behaviors (e.g., verbatim copying of the task intent in a single user utterance). For the evaluation, we used Qwen3.5-9B as the LLM judge for Quality, and the stronger GPT-5.6-Luna for Coverage, as we found this additional model capacity allowed to extract additional per-turn information about intent coverage.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Naturalness Metrics.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report naturalness using three complementary discriminators. We trained the first two discriminators in analogous ways to discriminators trained in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Training Details ‣ 3 Experimental Setup ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>. Both use ModernBert-Large as the base.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1. Naturalness-Specific:</span> We train a separate naturalness discriminator for each simulator to evaluate. The metric reports the average <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(y=\text{real}\mid\hat{u_{1}}...\hat{u_{k}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>real</mtext></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(y=\text{real}\mid\hat{u_{1}}...\hat{u_{k}})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\hat{u_{1}}...\hat{u_{k}}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\hat{u_{1}}...\hat{u_{k}}\}</annotation></semantics></math> is a simulated conversation on the test set.<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
                
                
                
              Note that unlike discriminator training in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Training Details ‣ 3 Experimental Setup ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>, we do not include input intents <math id="footnote3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> during discriminator training to avoid doubly penalizing conversations for coverage.</span></span></span> This is the strictest test for naturalness among our metrics as each discriminator specializes on patterns of individual simulators. For Human Reference interactions, we report average <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(y=\text{real}\mid u_{1}...u_{k})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>real</mtext></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(y=\text{real}\mid u_{1}...u_{k})</annotation></semantics></math> for real conversations <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{u_{1}...u_{k}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{u_{1}...u_{k}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, averaged over all model-specific discriminators.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2. Naturalness-General:</span> We train a general discriminator on data from all simulators, which includes our models, baselines from §<a href="#S3" title="3 Experimental Setup ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, and experiments with reward design alternatives in §<a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Reward Design Alternatives ‣ 4 Results and Analysis ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>.
This discriminator is generally less strict than the previous one, as it must distinguish between simulations from multiple distributions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3. Pangram:</span> As a dataset-agnostic discriminator, we use Pangram-4 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Glickenhaus et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, a state-of-the-art AI detection model trained to distinguish human and AI assistant text. We report Pangram’s recorded fraction of human-written text. For each intent, we randomly select one sampled conversation. To take into account’s Pangram’s limitations around short texts, we remove termination tags and concatenate a conversation’s user turns through the first whole turn that exceeds a cumulative <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math> words, or use all user turns if the conversation is shorter.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Naturalness Pass Rate (%).</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A conversation passes the overall naturalness criterion if at least one of the individual naturalness scores (specific, general, Pangram) is at or above <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math>. This pass rate represents the proportion of simulated conversations where at least one discriminator assigns majority probability to the conversation being classified as real (i.e., the discriminator is “fooled”).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Conversation Validity Metric.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We define an aggregate metric that measures whether a conversation passes <span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">both</span> task fidelity and naturalness expectations. This single, over-arching metric captures the proportion of conversations produced by a simulator that are usable for downstream purposes. Under our definition, a simulated conversation is valid if it meets four conditions: (1) a Quality score of <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>, (2) a Terminated score of <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>,<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
                
                
                
              Human Reference conversations count as terminated by construction.</span></span></span> (3) a Coverage score of at least <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.8</annotation></semantics></math>, and (4) passing the naturalness criterion. We also report estimated cost in USD per 100 valid conversations (lower is better), with base-model pricing proxies for fine-tuned models.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Evaluation results of user simulators. We compare prompted assistants (top), finetuned models (middle), and human reference conversations on task fidelity (Qual., Cov., Term.) and naturalness (component means Spec., Gen., Pan., and Naturalness Pass Rate, % Pass). We report overall conversation validity (Valid %) and estimated simulator cost in USD per 100 valid conversations.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Main Results</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present summarized evaluation metrics for task fidelity, naturalness, validity, and estimated simulation costs for UserLM-2.0 and baselines in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4 Results and Analysis ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparing prompted assistants and finetuned user simulators.</span> A general pattern emerges visually in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4 Results and Analysis ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Prompted assistants tend to achieve high coverage scores, but struggle to generate natural conversations.
For example, the best prompted assistant (GPT-5.6-Sol) achieves a naturalness pass rate of only 10.2%.
In contrast, most finetuned user simulators generally perform worse on coverage, but achieve much higher naturalness pass rates. UserLM-2.0 achieves optimal performance on both: it achieves the highest performance among simulators on coverage (88.0%) and naturalness pass rate (71.8%).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">UserLM-2.0 generates the highest proportion of valid simulations, outperforming the next-best model by <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{18.4\%}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">18.4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{18.4\%}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span> UserLM-2.0 achieves an overall validity score of 46.2%, which is 1.66 times as much as the next-best model (our finetuned UserLM-2.0-SFT, at a validity score of 27.8%) and 3.28 times as much as the best previously released user simulator (SFTUser-14B, at 14.1%). This means that, on average, UserLM-2.0  typically requires sampling two conversations to produce a valid one, when previous models required sampling at least 6, and often more than 15.
This, coupled with the small parameter count of UserLM-2.0, leads it to be the most cost-effective user simulator, costing $0.11 to generate 100 valid conversations, compared to $205.20 with GPT-5.6-Sol.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A large gap remains between simulated and real human–AI conversations.</span> The real, held-out human-AI conversations have perfect naturalness and near-perfect coverage, a 28.2% and 8.0% lead over the best user simulator (UserLM-2.0) on the two metrics respectively. This puts our results in perspective: UserLM-2.0 represents a significant step forward in user simulation, but there remains a substantial gap for future work to close. In particular, our RL-based methodology leads to a large improvement in the task fidelity of the initial SFT checkpoint without sacrificing its naturalness. However, improving beyond this initial naturalness to close the gap to real conversations remains an open challenge. Beyond the model artifact we release, we hope our evaluation methodology emphasizing validity of individual interactions can support future research in user simulation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Stress Testing Under Increasing Task Complexity</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Setup.</span> The key use-case for user simulators is supporting downstream evaluation and training. In particular, a user simulator must be capable of simulating realistic and valid interactions as task complexity varies. For evaluation purposes, we decomposed each test task intent into a set of <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">subgoals</span>: units of information that are part of the task intent. We argue that the number of subgoals of a task intent roughly correlates with task complexity, as more subgoals typically require longer conversation to convey, leading to more opportunity for user simulators to omit or contradict task information. As a first analysis, we break down the performance of user simulators as the number of subgoals increases. Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Stress Testing Under Increasing Task Complexity ‣ 4 Results and Analysis ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> reports coverage, naturalness pass rate, and overall validity against different levels of task intent complexity. We include similar tables for quality, termination, and individual naturalness scores in Appendix <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Task Complexity Stress-Test ‣ Appendix D Additional Analyses ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">UserLM-2.0 maintains the highest validity across all task-complexity levels.</span> The proportion of valid simulations generally declines as task complexity increases, but UserLM-2.0 leads all evaluated simulators at every level. At five sub-goals, it achieves 36.6% validity, compared with 11.3% for UserLM-2.0-SFT. At six and seven sub-goals, UserLM-2.0 retains validity rates of 23.6% and 12.6%, compared to below 1% for every prior simulator.</p>
</div>

We report mean Coverage, Naturalness Pass Rate (Naturalness Pass %), and overall Validity. Validity additionally requires quality and termination criteria. Scores are rounded to whole percentages.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Strong coverage alone does not ensure valid simulations.</span> UserLM-2.0 achieves near-perfect coverage for single-sub-goal tasks (99.4%) and the highest coverage among simulators for tasks with more than three sub-goals (Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Stress Testing Under Increasing Task Complexity ‣ 4 Results and Analysis ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). At seven sub-goals, it retains 79.4% coverage, compared with 78.0% for GPT-5.6-Luna, the strongest prompted assistant in this bucket, and 58.9% for UserLM-2.0-SFT. Yet GPT-5.6-Luna produces no valid simulations in this bucket, versus 12.6% for UserLM-2.0, illustrating why coverage and naturalness provide complementary views of performance.</p>
</div>
</section>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>Repetition and verbosity of user simulators. We report the rate of goal revisitation (Revisit), repetition-only turns (Rep. Only), goalless turns that do not advance the task intent (Emp.), and median user words per covered goal (W/goal). Rates are percentages; darker shading indicates closer agreement with humans for each metric.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For analysis purposes, we recorded which subgoal is revealed at which turn of simulated test conversations, offering a granular turn-by-turn signal to compare simulated conversation dynamics with real conversations. This allows us to perform three targeted analyses of simulator behavior in terms of repetition, verbosity, and turn dynamics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Behavioral Analysis of Simulators ‣ 4 Results and Analysis ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reports model performance on two repetition and two verbosity metrics (see Appendix <a href="#A3.SS5" title="C.5 Behavioral Metric Definitions ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Details ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.5</span></a> for exact definitions).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Repetition.</span> First off, human reference conversations tend to include a non-trivial amount of repetition, with 38.8% of subgoals repeated within a conversation, on average, and 33.3% of user turn utterances solely repeating information already provided. We find that UserLM-2.0 nearly matches the rates of information revisiting and repetition of human reference conversation (39.0% and 33.3%), whereas prompted assistants tend to repeat information (41.8–64.9%) and have non-progressing turns (35.8–57.4%) much more frequently.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Verbosity.</span> We label a turn as <span id="S4.SS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Empty</span> if it does not cover any subgoal. Such empty turns are relatively rare in real user conversations (6.9%) but are much more common in most finetuned simulators 18.6–50.5%, indicative of the tendency of finetuned simulators to go off script. UserLM-2.0 achieves low rates of empty turns (4.3%), comparable to human reference conversations and strong prompted assistants (3.6% for GPT-5.6-Sol). Looking at verbosity, we calculate the median number of words each simulator uses on average to reveal a subgoal (W/goal). Human reference conversations are remarkably concise (34 words/subgoal), 40% less than any simulator we tested. UserLM-2.0-SFT and UserLM-2.0 use a median of 54 and 59 words, respectively, significantly lower than all other simulators (77–315 words per subgoal). Thus, though UserLM-2.0 represents significant progress in terms of lowered verbosity, there remains a large gap with real users.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Goal-disclosure.</span> As a third analysis, we plot coverage progression over time. To enable direct comparisons against human reference conversations, we restrict our focus to conversations with at most six turns. For each turn, we compute the average cumulative coverage and proportion of newly introduced and repeated subgoals at that turn, which we plot in Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.3 Behavioral Analysis of Simulators ‣ 4 Results and Analysis ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Several patterns become apparent: first, when compared to human reference conversations, prompted assistants (GPT-5.6-Luna and DeepSeek-V4-Pro) tend to <span id="S4.SS3.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">front-load</span> task intent (i.e., reveal a much larger fraction of the entire task intent in the first turn) much more than real conversations (56% coverage at turn one in real conversations, vs. 70-77% for prompted assistants). Second, prompted assistants tend to repeat information excessively, whereas repetition is much sparser in real conversations. Finetuned simulators (UserLM-2.0-SFT and UserLM-8B) do not exhibit the same behavior of overly frontloading and repeating subgoals, but they do so at the cost of not achieving high coverage by the end of the conversation (80% and 68% coverage by end of conversation, respectively), affecting task fidelity and simulation validity. Finally, conversations simulated with UserLM-2.0 resemble real conversations the most in terms of conversation dynamics: less front-loading and repetition of information, while achieving the highest coverage by the end of the conversation (90%).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.31512v1/figures/pacing_analysis2.png" id="S4.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/289;" width="548" height="289" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>We depict goal disclosure over time for the Human Reference, UserLM-2.0,and prompted and finetuned baselines. Each bar represents the average cumulative coverage at a given conversation turn across sampled conversations. For each turn, the bolded component represents the proportion of newly covered sub-goals, while the gray component represents the proportion of revisited sub-goals. UserLM-2.0 achieves the best alignment with the Human Reference.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
