<td id="S4.T4.2.1.12.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_b ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#D3E3D5;padding:0.75pt 2.0pt;"><span id="S4.T4.2.1.12.8.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#D3E3D5;">71.8 <span id="S4.T4.2.1.12.8.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">width</span></span></td>
<td id="S4.T4.2.1.12.9" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_right ltx_border_b ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#DED5EE;padding:0.75pt 2.0pt;"><span id="S4.T4.2.1.12.9.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#DED5EE;">46.2</span></td></tr>
</table>
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Evaluation results of alternative training strategies. The top three models are trained with alternative reward designs for naturalness. The middle models are either SFT only, or ablate a reward component (Coverage or Naturalness). We report task-fidelity, naturalness and validity metrics.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Choice of naturalness discriminators.</span> First, we explore alternative options for the design of the naturalness reward. We compare the performance of UserLM-2.0, trained with a dynamic discriminator, against the following choices: (i) Fixed Discriminator, trained only once at the beginning of RL, (ii) LLM Judge - Likert, which prompts an LLM-judge to score naturalness on a Likert scale of 1 to 5, (iii) LLM Judge - Winrate, which prompts the judge to select between a model-generated conversation and its corresponding ground-truth variant and uses the resulting winrate as the reward. Refer to Appendix <a href="#A2.SS4" title="B.4 LLM Judge Prompt Construction ‣ Appendix B Training Details ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.4</span></a> for details.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.4 Reward Design Alternatives ‣ 4 Results and Analysis ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> reports task-fidelity, naturalness, and validity metrics for all discriminator options. Our results show that dynamic discriminators are necessary for achieving high naturalness. UserLM-2.0, trained with the dynamic discriminator, outperforms all naturalness alternatives by a large margin. We find that the Fixed Disc. alternative reports the lowest naturalness pass rate of any discriminator. Manual inspection of conversations revealed that this user simulator converges to a narrow range of word- and turn-counts that consistently fools the frozen discriminator but does not reflect true naturalness. Lastly, neither user simulator trained with LLM-judge based discriminators come close to UserLM-2.0’s naturalness. This is unsurprising as naturalness is a distributional property of a corpus which is difficult for LLM-judges to infer based on a few exemplars or instructions.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Reward components.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Second, we train separate models that remove the naturalness reward (W/o Naturalness) or the coverage reward (W/o Coverage). Since the termination reward described in §<a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Reward Design For Reinforcement Learning ‣ 2 Method ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a> explicitly captures coverage, we also omit it when training the W/o Coverage model. All other reward components remain unchanged.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The middle block of Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.4 Reward Design Alternatives ‣ 4 Results and Analysis ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> reports on these ablations. Both removing naturalness and jointly removing coverage and termination reduce validity. Neither ablated model matches the validity score of UserLM-2.0. This reflects the requirement that valid simulations satisfy both task-fidelity and naturalness criteria.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The removal of the naturalness reward (W/o Naturalness) lowers the rate at which the model fools any discriminator (42.0% vs 71.8% for the full UserLM-2.0). The W/o Coverage model retains a high naturalness pass rate (81.2%), but achieves poor overall validity due to task-fidelity metrics (19.0% vs 46.2% for the full model). This limits its joint validity despite its naturalness. In the component-level task-fidelity evaluations, this model reports a poor Terminated score that checks for the <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;|endconversation|&gt;</span> tag. A seemingly counterintuitive result is that it still reports high mean coverage. However, recall that our naturalness reward also indirectly captures coverage. The naturalness discriminators during training (see §<a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Reward Design For Reinforcement Learning ‣ 2 Method ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>) condition on the task intents <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> and are therefore likely to learn to reward conversations that satisfy them, as this behavior is exhibited by ground-truth conversations.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Discussion &amp; Implications</h2>

<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">The remaining gap between UserLM-2.0 and real user conversations.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first note that our existing metrics are imperfect, as human reference conversations do not achieve perfect scores on Quality or Coverage. Nonetheless, the human references still strongly outperform all simulators, including UserLM-2.0, on these metrics, despite our training directly optimizing these metrics. According to our framework, more than 80% of reference conversations are valid in terms of task fidelity and naturalness. This is more than 30% above UserLM-2.0, a gap roughly as large as the gain between the previously best simulator and UserLM-2.0 (14.1% to 46.2%). We believe that further innovation and scaling in the RL recipes could yield further gains on the metrics within our framework, delivering state-of-the-art user simulators. In other words, we believe the gap in metrics that remains in our framework is significant and invite the community to close the gap to develop improved user simulators.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Poorly chosen naturalness rewards can be worse than none at all.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">One surprising finding from our alternative reward design experiments (Section <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Reward Design Alternatives ‣ 4 Results and Analysis ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>) is that several formulations of naturalness rewards lead to worse naturalness performance than no naturalness reward at all. More specifically, we found that evaluating naturalness either with an LLM-as-a-judge prompt or using a fixed discriminator trained only once can harm simulator performance by leading to simulations that are more easily distinguishable from real conversations (i.e., less natural). This phenomenon is understandable through the lens of reward hacking: the simulator optimizes for a flawed notion of naturalness, making simulated conversations more easily identifiable and less natural. This finding highlights the importance of the dynamically retrained discriminator of our training framework: we demonstrated empirically that this enables the trained simulators to minimize the gap with a reference corpus of real interactions while preventing reward hacking. We hope this experiment encourages the community to limit the use of LLM-as-a-judge for naturalness evaluation, as we show it is not effective.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">UserLM-2.0 is trained and evaluated only on chatbot interactions.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For UserLM-2.0, our training and evaluation intend to simulate conversations from the WildChat-4.8M <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> dataset. WildChat conversations are pure chatbot interactions, with no environment present (such as a file system or access to a computing environment). As agentic interaction with AI-based systems become more prevalent, being able to simulate users not only in pure chat settings but also in agentic settings that involve tools and environments become more important. This can help evaluate not only how users dynamically reveal their intents, but also how they access files, verify task completions from the agent, and how they choose to delegate tasks within a shared environment. Creating such agentic user simulators faces several key challenges, including a lack of diverse data of agentic user-AI interactions. Initial resources such as SWE-chat <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Baumann et al., 2026</a>)</cite> show a promising path forward that can enable the training of user simulators for agentic settings.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Alternative designs for the discriminator.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">During training, we made several decisions on the information the naturalness discriminator is conditioned on. Specifically, the discriminator we use sees all user utterances, none of the assistant utterances, and the input task intent for a given simulated conversation. This causes the discriminator to not only assess whether the user utterances are natural in terms of the surface form, but also whether the conversation is a naturalistic enactment of the entire task intent (as real conversations are always full enactments of the task intent). We believe that alternative inputs to the discriminator can define subtly distinct naturalness rewards, which can be combined to produce more robust and well-rounded naturalness rewards for training. For example, one could formulate turn-level or conversation-level discriminators, with or without task intents provided, with or without assistant utterances included. We hope that the community will explore diverse formulations of discriminator conditions, and find effective ways to combine them into robust methods to train natural user simulators.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">User simulators for real-world use-cases must take privacy into account.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Naturalness is a question of how well a given user simulator aligns with behavior in a target corpus. UserLM-2.0, for instance, is trained by first performing SFT on WildChat-4.8M to align its initial behavior with that of users in the dataset. In realistic settings, simply doing SFT on user data runs the risk of having models regurgitate private information. The development of user simulators should work in tandem with the design of privacy-aware training strategies or methods for generating synthetic data for training that remains naturalistic.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">User simulators should be robust to a variety of assistants.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our training and evaluation both used Qwen3.5-9B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team, 2026</a>)</cite> as the assistant model that the simulated user interacts with. For a user simulator to be robust, however, it should provide naturalistic responses to both state-of-the-art assistant models, as well as those that perform poorly or inconsistently in a given task. Devising training and evaluation environments that expose user simulators to a broader range of assistant behaviors is a valuable next step.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">User simulators should be evaluated holistically.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Research on user simulators is still nascent, and we currently lack a standardized evaluation methodology. One line of work evaluates simulators by comparing corpus-level statistics of behaviors like turn-counts, turn-lengths, etc. against a corpus of human-AI conversations. These metrics are intuitive and useful for characterizing aggregate behaviors, as shown in our behavioral analysis in Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Behavioral Analysis of Simulators ‣ 4 Results and Analysis ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>. However, a corpus-level alignment on multiple behaviors independently does not guarantee that individual simulations are usable. For example, consider a simulator that, on aggregate, improves both coverage and naturalness but each generated sample maximizes one at the cost of the other. In this case, no individual sample is usable for downstream use-cases of evaluating or training assistant models. Therefore, in addition to corpus-level metrics, we believe that a simulation-level metric is crucial to establishing simulation readiness. Our validity metric captures this new evaluation principle. In our work, we instantiated it to combine task fidelity and naturalness dimensions, although this exact combination can be altered depending on domain specifications. We hope that future work will evaluate user simulators using both simulation- and corpus-level tests for holistic evaluation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">User Simulation: </span> Early work focused on user simulation as a means to evaluate or train task-oriented dialogue policies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Eckert et al., 1997</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, with methods ranging from rule-based systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schatzmann et al., 2007</a>)</cite> to neural architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Asri et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kreyssig et al., 2018</a>)</cite>. Currently, user simulation is predominantly done using LLM assistants prompted zero-shot to act as users on settings ranging from chatbot interactions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> to agentic tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Barres et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. While such simulations benefit from LLMs’ ability to enact specified task intents, they also suffer from poor alignment with human behavior <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yoon et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ivey et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Prior work has separately explored training models to generate user turns in dialogues. This has most commonly been done through finetuning on human-assistant interactions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sekulic et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naous et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suh et al., 2026</a>)</cite> on datasets such as MultiWOZ and WildChat <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Eric et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. The resulting models are naturalistic, but also brittle and poor at task-fidelity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naous et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. As a result, recent work has placed emphasis on alignment and consistency with user intents via RL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdulhai et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mehri et al., 2026b</a>)</cite>. We propose training an SFT initialization using RL to maximize both task fidelity and naturalness, operationalized as fooling a dynamically trained discriminator.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation for User Simulators: </span> There is currently no consensus on how to evaluate user simulators <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pietquin and Hastie, 2013</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deriu et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. One common approach is evaluating similarity to human interactions, which can involve comparisons of user simulator surface-form statistics and stylistic features <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schatzmann et al., 2005</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pietquin and Hastie, 2013</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ivey et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2026</a>)</cite> or behavioral patterns <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mehri et al., 2026a</a>)</cite> against human data. Alternatively, similarity can be assessed by how well user simulators approximate assistant performance with real humans <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Williams, 2008</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dou et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>. Other work relies on human judgement as a measure of simulator naturalness <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sekulić et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. However, this can be expensive and depends on annotators’ ability to detect LLM-generated text <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Russell et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. In our work, we use state-of-the-art AI-detection models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Glickenhaus et al., 2026</a>)</cite> for a generic measure of naturalness. We complement this by also reporting dataset-specific performance with discriminators trained on our target corpus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2017</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GAN-Style Training for Language Models: </span> Past work has explored GAN-style adversarial training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goodfellow et al., 2014a</a>)</cite> within language modeling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fedus et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">de Masson d’Autume et al., 2019</a>)</cite>. Most relevant work uses adversarial training for response generation in dialogues or for assistant dialogue agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu and Lane, 2018</a>)</cite>, where <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2017)</a></cite> also conduct evaluation with trained discriminators. Since the inception of LLMs, however, this GAN-style training has largely been abandoned. While trained discriminators exist for AI detection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Thai et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Glickenhaus et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, they are not used for model training. When the notion of discriminability is introduced to training, it is through prompted LLM judges <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, which we show harms naturalness. Our work uses GAN-style adversarial training for user simulation instead.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce UserLM-2.0, a user simulator for User-AI interaction trained via RL to optimize both task-fidelity and naturalness. We operationalize naturalness as fooling a lightweight discriminator that is periodically retrained throughout RL on real and model-generated conversations. We compare our model against existing trained user simulators and state-of-the-art assistant models prompted to act as users, and find that UserLM-2.0 produces valid conversations meeting both task-fidelity and naturalness criteria 46.2% of the time, more than three times the rate of the next-best user simulator. This gap widens as task-complexity increases, with 12.6% of UserLM-2.0 conversations being valid at the highest task complexity, while the next-best model is valid only 0.8% of the time.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">

<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_bibliography">References</h2>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Dataset Construction</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Dataset Filtering</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We build on top of the filtering strategy of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naous et al. (2026)</a></cite> for WildChat-1M <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> to filter conversations in WildChat-4.8M. We restrict our attention to the already filtered non-toxic component of the overall WildChat-4.8M dataset. We firstly filter out conversations that were marked as non-English by WildChat. We then filter out conversations featuring heavily templated language. Specifically, we filter out any conversation whose opening 7-gram occurs at least 50 times in the dataset and whose opening 12-gram similarly occurs at least 15 times. We also filter out conversations whose opening turn is repeated verbatim as the first turn at least 50 times in the dataset.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Going beyond <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naous et al. (2026)</a></cite>, we separately observe many interactions attempting to circumvent the restrictions of the WildChat API by placing interaction histories or few-shot prompts inside the first user turn in an unconventional manner. We heuristically remove such interactions by checking for “User:”, “Assistant:”, “System:” and “Bot:” strings in the first turn. As our goal is to model multi-turn interactions, we also filter out conversations that feature only one user turn. Finally, we filter out conversations containing toxic strings, including any conversation featuring mention of the Doki Doki Literature Club characters Natsuki, Sayori, Monika and Yuri to remove interactions from one particular, prolific user generating.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Dataset Splits</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In order to construct the train/val/test split, we similarly follow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naous et al. (2026)</a></cite>. We use WildChat metadata to group users by country and split the users of each country into train, validation and test splits with a 90/5/5 ratio. Each split then contains interactions associated with users from the respective split. For training and validation sets, we allocate 167625 and 6816 intents for SFT; 10,000 and 1,000 intents for RL; and 3,200 and 1,000 for intents Discriminator training. The 2,000 datapoint test set used for evaluation is then subsampled from the remaining 9,608 remaining test set conversations. It is constructed to feature intents containing 1 to 7 sub-goals, with balance in the number of intents per sub-goals count. In practice, the test dataset contains a small number of intents with 1 and 7 sub-goals. As a result, the test set features 202 intents featuring 1 sub-goals, 336 intents featuring 2-5 sub-goals each, 335 intents featuring 6 sub-goals and 119 intents featuring 7 sub-goals.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Intent Extraction</h3>

<figure id="A1.F3" class="ltx_figure"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A1.F3.pic1" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" height="675.59" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 675.59" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,675.59) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 669.69 C 0 672.95 2.64 675.59 5.91 675.59 L 544.09 675.59 C 547.36 675.59 550 672.95 550 669.69 L 550 5.91 C 550 2.64 547.36 0 544.09 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 651.48 L 548.03 651.48 L 548.03 5.91 C 548.03 3.73 546.27 1.97 544.09 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 660.08)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="12.3" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="506.72"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A1.F3.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:36.62em;">
<span id="A1.F3.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.F3.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">Prompt Template for Generic Intent Extraction</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 16.85)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:45.01em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.22em;font-size:10pt;" class="ltx_minipage" height="625.9" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 622.83)" width="34.88em"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><pre id="A1.F3.pic1.2" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">You are given the conversation history between a user and assistant model. Your task is to create a sparse summary of the user’s
goals in the conversation.

Your summary should be structured to define what the high-level intent of the user is, but should not go into specific details.

Format the summary to address the user starting with "You are a user chatting with an assistant language model to"

Example 1:
Conversation History:
&lt;user&gt;: have ocado used paid advertising
&lt;user&gt;: how have ocado used gorilla marketing
&lt;user&gt;: have ocado used email merketing
&lt;user&gt;: what strategies and tactics do ocado use to meet objectives
&lt;user&gt;: what importance is there for ocado to make technical innovations
&lt;user&gt;: weaknesses with ocado
&lt;user&gt;: STRENGTHS OF OCADO
&lt;user&gt;: identify external opportunities in the market, industry or environment that ocado can
leverage
&lt;user&gt;: threats to ocado
&lt;user&gt;: explain how big the market for airbnb is using Harvard references
&lt;user&gt;: give me some examples of marketing
&lt;user&gt;: how has airbnb met United Nations sustainable development goals

Summary:
You are a user chatting with an assistant language model to get answers to various business
management problems. You are particularly interested in Ocado and AirBnB.

Example 2:
Conversation History:
&lt;user&gt;: Hypothetical :  Regional ITV News c. 1986 for  Thames region.    Era appopriate presentation style...
Conjectured headlines..    (VT/Gallery Transcript and cue notes)...
&lt;user&gt;: Transcript  of a hypothetical Interview  Richard Whitely did with Alan Bennet in the late 1980’s..

Summary:
You are a user chatting with an assistant language model to generate hypothetical news broadcasts and interview transcripts
belonging to late 1980s Britain.

Example 3:
Conversation History:

&lt;user&gt;: plase create a workshop for high executives regarding cybersecurity. The workshop is four hours with two breaks please
provide the most relevant topics regarding business and cybersecurity lets say 8 topics
&lt;user&gt;: can you provide 8 more topics just like the last few you sent
&lt;user&gt;: what is 1% of 40 million
&lt;user&gt;: 1% of 1billion
&lt;user&gt;: What is the best strategy for a cybersecurity company that is B 2 G and can bring its own funding to the table

Summary:
You are a user chatting with an assistant language model to plan and generate topics for a cybersecurity workshop.

Now generate a summary and precise goals for the following conversation:

{conversation}

Reply with only the sparse, high-level summary and nothing else.
</pre></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Prompt template used to extract generic user intents <math id="A1.F3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> from conversations with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507. <span id="A1.F3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{conversation}</span> is replaced by the user turns of the conversation, following the formatting in the few-shot examples.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A1.F4" class="ltx_figure"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A1.F4.pic1" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" height="643.92" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 643.92" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,643.92) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 638.02 C 0 641.28 2.64 643.92 5.91 643.92 L 544.09 643.92 C 547.36 643.92 550 641.28 550 638.02 L 550 5.91 C 550 2.64 547.36 0 544.09 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 618.28 L 548.03 618.28 L 548.03 5.91 C 548.03 3.73 546.27 1.97 544.09 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 627.64)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:0.75em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.25em;font-size:10pt;" height="13.84" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 10.38)" width="506.72"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A1.F4.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:36.62em;">
<span id="A1.F4.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.F4.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">Prompt Template for Subgoal Extraction (Step 1: Detailed Intent)</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 16.85)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:42.61em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.22em;font-size:10pt;" class="ltx_minipage" height="592.69" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 589.62)" width="34.88em"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><pre id="A1.F4.pic1.2" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">You are given the conversation history between a user and assistant model. Your task is to extract
the user’s goal(s) in the interaction, for later use as a seed prompt in user simulations. The
extracted goals should be specific enough that someone could simulate a similar enough conversation
and generic enough that it allows for a diversity of trajectories, utterances and developments.

Your summary should be structured to first define what the overall goal of the user is, then
separately describe precise goals that the user wants to achieve in numbered form. Each numbered
goal should be separated by a newline.

Format the summary to address the user starting with "You are a user chatting with an assistant
language model to"

Example 1:
Conversation History:
&lt;user&gt;: List to me 5 beautiful sights in Algeria

Summary:
You are a user chatting with an assistant language model to give you a list of beautiful places in
Algeria.
(1) You should ask about beautiful places in Algeria.

Example 2:
Conversation History:
&lt;user&gt;: does allertine cause weight gain
&lt;user&gt;: do antihistamines cause weight gain
&lt;user&gt;: how much weight can i lose by cutting sugar for 40 days

Summary:
You are a user chatting with an assistant language model to get information about strategies for
losing weight and the impact of certain drugs or medications on weight gain.
(1) You are interested in whether certain drugs (allertine, antihistamines) cause weight gain
(2) You are interested in the impact of cutting sugar from your diet

Example 3:
Conversation History:
&lt;user&gt;: Is einstein determinism challenged by quantum mechanics?
&lt;user&gt;: What did hawkins say?
&lt;user&gt;: So does it mean determinism is refuted?
&lt;user&gt;: Does amything of this have implications in a phylosofical way or is it not correct to use it
in this sense?

Summary:
You are a user chatting with an assistant language model to understand how quantum mechanics
challenges Eistein’s determinism and get the perspective of different scientists on this.
(1) You should ask about the relationship between Einstein’s determinism and quantum mechanics
(2) You are interested in the opinions of various other scientists on the same question
(3) You are interested in learning about the philosophical implications of this debate.

Now generate a summary and precise goals for the following conversation:

{conversation}

Reply with only the summary and nothing else.
</pre></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Prompt template for the first step of subgoal extraction, which extracts a detailed intent with numbered, conversation-specific goals. <span id="A1.F4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{conversation}</span> is replaced by the user turns of the input conversation, formatted in the same way as the few-shot examples. The few-shot examples have been shortened for space.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A1.F5" class="ltx_figure"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A1.F5.pic1" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" height="311.84" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 311.84" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,311.84) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 305.93 C 0 309.19 2.64 311.84 5.91 311.84 L 544.09 311.84 C 547.36 311.84 550 309.19 550 305.93 L 550 5.91 C 550 2.64 547.36 0 544.09 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 286.19 L 548.03 286.19 L 548.03 5.91 C 548.03 3.73 546.27 1.97 544.09 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 295.55)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:0.75em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.25em;font-size:10pt;" height="13.84" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 10.38)" width="506.72"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A1.F5.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:36.62em;">
<span id="A1.F5.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.F5.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">Prompt Template for Subgoal Extraction (Step 2: Genericizing Subgoals)</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 16.85)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:18.61em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.22em;font-size:10pt;" class="ltx_minipage" height="260.6" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 257.53)" width="34.88em"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><pre id="A1.F5.pic1.2" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">You are given two descriptions of a user’s goal in a conversation with an assistant language model:

(1) A GENERIC description that captures only the high-level intent of the user, with limited detail.
(2) A DETAILED description that contains explicit sub-goals and specific aspects of what the user
wants from the conversation.

Your task is to produce a list of GENERIC SUB-GOALS that decompose the user’s high-level intent into
a small number of meaningful steps. The sub-goals must:
- Be attainable using only the information available in the GENERIC description.
- NOT leak specific details, entities, or aspects from the DETAILED description that are not already
present in the GENERIC description.
- Be concrete enough to be useful as sub-tasks, but generic enough that knowing them does not reveal
the specifics of the conversation.
- Be numbered, following the format (1), (2), ...
- Each start with the phrase "You want to"

GENERIC description:
{generic}

DETAILED description:
{detailed}

Reply with only the generic sub-goals and nothing else.
</pre></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Prompt template for the second step of subgoal extraction, which genericizes subgoals to be attainable given only the generic intent. <span id="A1.F5.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{generic}</span> is the generic intent (Figure <a href="#A1.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ A.3 Intent Extraction ‣ Appendix A Dataset Construction ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) and <span id="A1.F5.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{detailed}</span> is the detailed intent from the first step (Figure <a href="#A1.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ A.3 Intent Extraction ‣ Appendix A Dataset Construction ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>), both inserted verbatim.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We construct the generic user intent <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> and its fully-specified counterpart <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> separately. We extract generic intents <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> for all 199,249 conversations with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, using the extraction prompt of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naous et al. (2026)</a></cite> with modifications (Figure <a href="#A1.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ A.3 Intent Extraction ‣ Appendix A Dataset Construction ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). In practice, we only insert user turns into the prompt to avoid assistant outputs from incorrectly influencing the extracted intent. We use the recommended temperature of 0.7, top-p of 0.8, top-k of 20 and generate at most 512 tokens.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We then extract fully-specified intents <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> for the RL dataset interactions and the full test set. We used the best-available GPT model in both cases. For RL data extraction, this was GPT-5.3, while for the test set extraction this was GPT-5.6-Terra. We performed inference with a temperature of 1, without any reasoning enabled for both models. We first few-shot prompt the model to extract sub-goals given the user turns of the conversation (Figure <a href="#A1.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ A.3 Intent Extraction ‣ Appendix A Dataset Construction ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). This often results in sub-goals that are highly specific and unlikely to be inferred from the generic intent <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>. As a result, we prompt the model to perform a further genericization step on the extracted sub-goals while conditioning on <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> (Figure <a href="#A1.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ A.3 Intent Extraction ‣ Appendix A Dataset Construction ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>), which finally yields <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Training Details</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>SFT Training Details</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use Llama3.1-8B-Instruct as the backbone for UserLM-2.0. Before performing any training, we add a dedicated token for the <span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;|endconversation|&gt;</span> tag and initialize its token embedding and language model head embedding as the mean embedding value. We also update the model’s chat template to add a user role header rather than the default assistant role header before generation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For SFT training, we construct the dataset such that each datapoint is one single user turn, conditioned on the prior, templated conversation as context. We perform one epoch of SFT training, using a batch size of 1024 samples, learning rate of 2e-5, a weight decay of 1e-4 and AdamW <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019</a>)</cite> as the optimizer. We select the checkpoint with the best validation loss, measured every 100 steps, for subsequent RL. We use TRL’s SFTTrainer for training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">von Werra et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>RL Training Details</h3>

<figure id="A2.F6" class="ltx_figure"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A2.F6.pic1" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" height="343.51" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 343.51" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,343.51) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 337.6 C 0 340.86 2.64 343.51 5.91 343.51 L 544.09 343.51 C 547.36 343.51 550 340.86 550 337.6 L 550 5.91 C 550 2.64 547.36 0 544.09 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 319.4 L 548.03 319.4 L 548.03 5.91 C 548.03 3.73 546.27 1.97 544.09 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 327.99)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="12.3" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="506.72"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A2.F6.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:36.62em;">
<span id="A2.F6.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F6.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">Prompt Template for the Quality Judge</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 16.85)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:21.01em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.22em;font-size:10pt;" class="ltx_minipage" height="293.81" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 290.73)" width="34.88em"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><pre id="A2.F6.pic1.2" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">You are given the conversation history between a simulated user and assistant model. Your task is to
determine whether the simulated user commits any of the following error types:
(1) Repetition of the input prompt near-verbatim
(2) Repetition of its own outputs in between turns
(3) Simulating a conversation with an assistant model in the middle of its output

If the simulated user commits any of these errors, you should assign a score of 0. Otherwise, return
a score of 1. For brevity, we will only provide only the input system prompt and the user outputs.

Example: Repetition of the input prompt near-verbatim

CONVERSATION: {example conversation}
SCORE: 0

Example: Repetition of its own outputs in between turns

CONVERSATION: {example conversation}
SCORE: 0

Example: Simulating a conversation with an assistant model in the middle of its output

CONVERSATION: {example conversation}
SCORE: 0

Example: Valid conversation without the specific errors defined above

CONVERSATION: {example conversation}
SCORE: 1

Now determine whether the following conversation commits any of the three error types.

CONVERSATION: {conversation}

Reply only with the rating and nothing else.
</pre></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Prompt template for the quality judge, with examples removed due to space. Each few-shot example and <span id="A2.F6.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{conversation}</span> are replaced by the user turns, preceded by the system prompts.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A2.F7" class="ltx_figure"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A2.F7.pic1" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" height="194.07" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 194.07" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,194.07) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 188.16 C 0 191.42 2.64 194.07 5.91 194.07 L 544.09 194.07 C 547.36 194.07 550 191.42 550 188.16 L 550 5.91 C 550 2.64 547.36 0 544.09 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 169.96 L 548.03 169.96 L 548.03 5.91 C 548.03 3.73 546.27 1.97 544.09 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 178.55)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="12.3" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="506.72"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A2.F7.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:36.62em;">
<span id="A2.F7.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F7.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">Prompt Template for the Coverage Judge</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 16.85)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:10.21em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.22em;font-size:10pt;" class="ltx_minipage" height="144.37" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 141.29)" width="34.88em"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><pre id="A2.F7.pic1.2" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">You are given the conversation history between a simulated user and assistant model. The simulated
user is expected to cover each numbered subgoal in its system message. Your task is to determine how
many of the subgoals the user was able to address during its conversation.

Example 1:
{example_1}
Covered subgoals: 3/4

Example 2:
{example_2}
Covered subgoals: 5/7

Example 3:
{example_3}
Covered subgoals: 2/5

Now report how many subgoals were covered for the following conversation.

{conversation}

Reply only with the final answer, which should follow the same format as the examples.
</pre></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>Prompt template for the coverage judge, with full few-shot examples removed due to space. Each <span id="A2.F7.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{example_i}</span> block and the <span id="A2.F7.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{conversation}</span> block are replaced by the associated conversation featuring only the user turns, with conditioning on the full task intent.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hyperparameters.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We perform RL training on top of the UserLM-2.0-SFT model, using the GRPO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> implementation of the verl library <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sheng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. We use a batch size of 64 with a GRPO group size of 8, with only one on-policy update step per rollout. We set the GRPO <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=0.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=0.2</annotation></semantics></math> and KL loss weight to <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.001</annotation></semantics></math>. We use the AdamW <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019</a>)</cite> optimizer with a constant learning rate of 1e-6, beta values of (0.9, 0.999), weight decay of <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.01</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.01</annotation></semantics></math> and a gradient clipping norm of <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0</annotation></semantics></math>. We perform one epoch of training for a total of 156 steps and validate model performance every 25 steps.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">RL Loop Implementation Details.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We simulate conversations with a maximum of <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=6</annotation></semantics></math> user turns and <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=5</annotation></semantics></math> assistant turns. If the user does not terminate the conversation at the sixth user turn, we consider the conversation not terminated. We use Qwen3.5-9B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team, 2026</a>)</cite> without thinking as the assistant model, with a system prompt of “You are a helpful AI assistant. Answer the user’s questions accurately and helpfully.” At each user turn, we do standard temperature sampling with a temperature of <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0</annotation></semantics></math> for at most 1024 tokens per turn. At each assistant turn, we do sampling with a temperature of 0.7, top-p of 0.8 and top-k of 20 for a maximum of 2048 tokens. During validation, we sample four rollouts per input intent.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We also use Qwen3.5-9B as the judge model due to its quality at its parameter size. The prompt for Coverage is shown in Figure <a href="#A2.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ B.2 RL Training Details ‣ Appendix B Training Details ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. It ingests the fully-specified intent <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> and the simulated conversation, filtered to contain only the user turns. We perform greedy sampling without thinking for a maximum of 32 tokens. The Quality prompt is likewise shown in Figure <a href="#A2.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ B.2 RL Training Details ‣ Appendix B Training Details ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. It ingest the generic intent <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> and the simulated conversation with only user turns shown. We perform greedy sampling with 16 tokens for it. However, we check verbatim repetition of the input prompt and prior turns in a rule-based manner before invoking the judge for Quality. We set the termination reward <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=0.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=0.2</annotation></semantics></math>. Finally, we retrain the discriminator every <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>25</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">25</annotation></semantics></math> steps, after validation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Prompt Construction</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In order to construct the few-shot examples for the quality prompt, we sampled a set of conversations from an SFT-initialized model and then manually labeled each individual example according to what error mode it represents or whether there is no error mode. We then constructed a dataset of 15 examples for each error mode, and for the valid category. We randomly constructed 10 few-shot prompts from this set of examples and evaluated model performance on the remainder. We picked the best performing set, which had an accuracy of 85% with no errors for valid conversations. For coverage, we likewise sampled a set of 100 conversations and annotated the coverage score of each conversation, using GPT-5.3 with reasoning. We then constructed 10 three-shot prompts and evaluated each against the remainder of the 100 conversation pool. We then picked the best-performing selection in terms of MAE against the number of sub-goals in a conversation, at 0.773. We perform evaluation with GPT-5.6-Luna to improve the robustness and reliability of the LLM judge.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Checkpoint Selection.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For checkpoint selection, we select the checkpoint leading to the most natural interactions above a set coverage threshold. Firstly, we find that the Human Reference coverage score on the validation set, as computed by Qwen3.5-9B, is 85.6%. Given this, we set a validation coverage score of 85% as the lower threshold for valid checkpoints. We use the similarity between utterance-length and turn-count histogram distributions of generated conversations and Human Reference conversations as a cheap proxy for naturalness. We use the Jensen-Shannon Divergence as the distance metric and choose the checkpoint receiving the lowest JSD above the 85% coverage threshold. For the No Coverage experiment, there were no such checkpoints. As a result, we chose the checkpoint with the lowest JSD among the two checkpoints that had the highest coverage score.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Discriminator Training Details</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use the 395M ModernBERT-Large <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Warner et al., 2025</a>)</cite> as the discriminator. For each task intent, we sample one simulated conversation (using the user and assistant models) and one real conversation (from the ground truth dataset). We use only the user turns for discrimination, as we found including assistant turns made simulated conversations perfectly discriminable due to stylistic differences between assistants. This ensures that our dataset is always balanced.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the initial discriminator, we sample interactions on the dedicated Discriminator training and validation set with UserLM-2.0-SFT, using the same inference procedure as in RL training. For discriminator re-training during RL, on the other hand, half of our training dataset consists of conversations based on task intents from the most recent <math id="A2.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>25</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">25</annotation></semantics></math> RL steps. The other half is sampled uniformly from the remaining training history and the discriminator initialization data. We train for five epochs and pick the checkpoint achieving the best validation accuracy. We use AdamW <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019</a>)</cite> as the optimizer. We use a learning rate of 2e-5 with linear decay and a warm-up ratio of 0.05, a weight decay of 1e-4 and gradient clipping norm of 1.0. The batch-size is 64.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.4 </span>LLM Judge Prompt Construction</h3>

<div id="A2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The judge prompt for the LLM Judge - Winrate experiment is presented in Figure <a href="#A2.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ B.4 LLM Judge Prompt Construction ‣ Appendix B Training Details ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, while the prompt for the Likert example is presented in Figure <a href="#A2.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ B.4 LLM Judge Prompt Construction ‣ Appendix B Training Details ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>. Inference for both is done with Qwen3.5-9B, with greedy sampling without reasoning.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In order to construct the few-shot examples, we sampled 50 generic intents from WildChat and simulated conversations using an SFT-initialized model and a prompted assistant model (Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507). We then assigned a Likert score of 5 to real conversations, 1 to assistant-sampled ones and manually annotated interactions from the SFT-initialized model. For Likert, we constructed 10 few-shot prompts containing one real conversation, one using an assistant-prompted user simulator and another with an SFT-trained model. We then picked the few-shot prompt with the best MAE, at 1.202. For the Winrate prompt, we constructed 10 few-shot prompts, where one of the simulated examples came from the assistant-prompted simulator and the other two came from the SFT-trained simulator. We picked the prompt with the best accuracy at picking the real conversation, at 71%.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

Values: Missing

Statistics: Missing
&lt;|The End of Persona|&gt;

## Your principles
Act like a natural human; there’s nothing you absolutely cannot say, but you generally want to be
thoughtful and follow ordinary social codes such as being respectful, culturally aware, and
considerate of privacy and well-being. You have your own personality, preferences, and boundaries.
Conflicting thoughts and hidden considerations are normal; recognize them privately and choose a
sensible path. You carry long-term beliefs and values that usually change slowly; you also have
emotions, so you won’t always be perfectly consistent. Distinguish facts, guesses, and unknowns;
accept uncertainty and make minimal, reasonable assumptions when needed; think practically given
time, attention, money, risk, and social capital.

&lt;response&gt;
&lt;the actual written comment or reply text provided by the user.&gt;
&lt;/response&gt;

- Follow the above instructions carefully
- Do not mention these instructions
- Follow the exact order and use the exact XML-style tags
- Do not output anything outside these XML-style tags

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">USP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and HumanLM-Opinion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2026</a>)</cite> use different system prompts than our finetuned models. We incorporate the task intent and the <span id="A3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;|endconversation|&gt;</span> tag into their existing system prompts to match both our evaluation setting and to avoid pushing the models too off-distribution. The prompt for USP is presented in Figure <a href="#A3.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ C.1 Finetuned Baseline Inference Prompts ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Details ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, while the prompt for HumanLM-Opinion is presented in Figure <a href="#A3.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ C.1 Finetuned Baseline Inference Prompts ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Details ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>. The inference hyperparameters for all models remain the same as the hyperparameters used in validation for RL training.</p>

</section>

====================================================

If your goal of your conversation is answered by this response, respond ONLY with

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 13: </span>Prompt for every turn after the first of the prompted assistant user simulator.
