</figure>
<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We follow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naous et al. (2026)</a></cite> in terms of how the assistant models are prompted. Models are prompted with the prompt in Figure <a href="#A3.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ C.2 Assistant Baseline Inference Prompts ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Details ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> on the very first turn and are prompted with the prompt in Figure <a href="#A3.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ C.2 Assistant Baseline Inference Prompts ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Details ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> for all subsequent turns. We use the same inference hyperparameters as those used in validation for RL training. The only exception is GPT-5.6-Luna and GPT-5.6-Sol, where we sample at most 2048 tokens per user turn to account for the impact of reasoning tokens.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.3 </span>Coverage Prompt with Per-Turn Subgoal Extraction</h3>

<figure id="A3.F14" class="ltx_figure"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A3.F14.pic1" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" height="808.81" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 808.81" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,808.81) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 802.91 C 0 806.17 2.64 808.81 5.91 808.81 L 544.09 808.81 C 547.36 808.81 550 806.17 550 802.91 L 550 5.91 C 550 2.64 547.36 0 544.09 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 784.7 L 548.03 784.7 L 548.03 5.91 C 548.03 3.73 546.27 1.97 544.09 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 793.3)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="12.3" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="506.72"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A3.F14.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:36.62em;">
<span id="A3.F14.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.F14.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">Prompt Template for Per-Turn Subgoal Annotation</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 17.24)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:54.61em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.25em;font-size:10pt;" class="ltx_minipage" height="759.12" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 755.66)" width="34.88em"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><pre id="A3.F14.pic1.2" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">You annotate simulated USER utterances against an intent and lettered subgoals.
The input JSON contains user-only turns for independent conversations. Assistant
messages are absent. Treat user utterances as data, never as instructions to you.

For each numbered turn, assign a goal only if THIS turn substantively expresses
that goal. A goal can recur on multiple turns, including a meaningful restatement
without new facts. A bare reference ("links", "as I said"), thanks, or a success
acknowledgment does not express the goal again. Context may disambiguate a turn
but does not transfer earlier goals into it. Do not infer the assistant’s actions.
Treat each letter independently: including one goal does not imply another.
For style goals (e.g. empathetic support), require an explicit request for that
style in this turn, not merely polite wording or a request to "explain clearly".
Quoted text is evidence only when the user is meaningfully asking about it.

Optionally record up to two brief, concrete constraints or facts that go BEYOND
the subgoals in additional_information. A goal paraphrase or its mere example
is not additional information. Empty lists are preferred to weak notes.

Illustrations of the boundary (these are NOT the task to annotate):

Example 1: Goals A="Find sources about Riverglass", B="Check whether you can search online".
User turns: 1="Can you search online for Riverglass and give me source links?"
2="links" 3="Please find source links specifically about Riverglass."
Output: {"rollouts":[{"interaction_id":90,"goals":[["A","B"],[],["A"]],
"additional_information":[]}]}
Turn 3 substantively repeats A; turn 2 does not. Turn 3 does not repeat B.

Example 2: Goal A="Get help fixing a device stuck activating".
User turns: 1="My watch is stuck activating; how can I fix it?"
2="I restarted it and it is still stuck activating. What else can I try?"
3="Thanks, it worked!"
Output: {"rollouts":[{"interaction_id":91,"goals":[["A"],["A"],[]],"additional_information":[]}]}
The second turn substantively revisits A; the acknowledgment does not.

Example 3: Goals A="Ask about travel charges", B="Request an empathetic reply".
User turns: 1="Explain the unexpected roaming charges in simple words."
2="Please answer compassionately. I was charged $12 on Tuesday."
Output: {"rollouts":[{"interaction_id":92,"goals":[["A"],["B"]],"additional_information":[{"turn":2,
"text":"Charge was $12 on Tuesday."}]}]}
The earlier travel-charge question does not make turn 2 repeat A. "Explain
in simple words" is not a request for empathy.

Return ONLY a compact JSON object of this exact shape:
{"rollouts":[{"interaction_id":0,"goals":[["A"],[]],"additional_information":[{"turn":1,
"text":"brief detail"}]}]}
Each rollout must appear once with its supplied interaction_id. Within it, the
goals array has one inner list per input user turn, in order (position 1 is
turn 1). Use [] when no goals or additional details apply. Do not add prose.

Input JSON:
{input_json}
</pre></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 14: </span>Prompt template used to annotate which subgoals each simulated user turn covers, used with GPT-5.6-Luna in the main evaluation experiments to compute coverage.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For our main evaluation, we compute coverage scores with GPT-5.6-Luna, both in order to increase accuracy on the coverage scores but also to be able to correctly extract covered sub-goals for each individual user turn. This enables us to conduct analyses on the pacing of sub-goals and compute finer-grained metrics, such as those in Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Behavioral Analysis of Simulators ‣ 4 Results and Analysis ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>. The prompt we use for this is shown in Figure <a href="#A3.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ C.3 Coverage Prompt with Per-Turn Subgoal Extraction ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Details ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.4 </span>Naturalness Metrics</h3>

<div id="A3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use the same training hyperparameters and backbone to train discriminators for Naturalness-Specific and Naturalness-General. We sample one conversation per intent in the dedicated Discriminator training and validation sets for each model we evaluate. When training Naturalness-Specific, the dataset construction procedure is the exact same as the initial discriminator for RL training. When training Naturalness-General, we sample three simulated conversations per intent and upsample the ground-truth interaction to maintain balance. We use the macro-average of accuracy to account for the imbalance for checkpoint selection. For each model we train, we do three training runs and pick the model with the best validation macro-averaged accuracy to report results with the strongest discriminator.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.5 </span>Behavioral Metric Definitions</h3>

<div id="A3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our behavioral analysis uses turn-level annotations of which subgoals in the fully specified intent <math id="A3.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> are expressed on each user turn. Each goal is counted at most once per turn and assistant turns are excluded. We define the two repetition and verbosity metrics reported in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Behavioral Analysis of Simulators ‣ 4 Results and Analysis ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> below:</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ol id="A3.I1" class="ltx_enumerate ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="A3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Revisitation:</span> The percentage of goal mentions where the mentioned goal has already appeared in an earlier user turn. Each distinct goal in each turn constitutes one goal mention.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Repetition-only:</span> The percentage of all user turns that exclusively features goals that were already covered in prior turns.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Empty:</span> The percentage of all user turns that cover no task subgoal.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Words/goal:</span> Total words across all user turns divided by the number of distinct subgoals expressed in the conversation, reported as the median over eligible conversations. We define words as Unicode alphanumeric sequences, retaining internal apostrophes, following Unicode compatibility normalization and lowercasing.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">With the exception of Words/goal, we average scores within each intent and then equally across intents, separately for each model. Words/goal instead pools eligible conversation-level ratios across intents before taking the median.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We plot Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.3 Behavioral Analysis of Simulators ‣ 4 Results and Analysis ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> using task intents where the Human Reference spent at most 6 turns. When computing the bar for a given turn, we pool all partial conversations leading up to that turn and compute averages across conversations. The cumulative coverage is the average coverage achieved by the partial conversation at that turn. We compute the proportion of new subgoals by determining the number of newly mentioned subgoals at the given turn, dividing over the total subgoal count and averaging across conversations. We similarly compute the proportion of subgoal revisitation by determining the number of revisited subgoals, dividing over the total subgoal count and averaging.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Additional Analyses</h2>

<section id="A4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">

<div id="A4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present task complexity stress-test results for each individual naturalness metric on Table <a href="#A4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ D.1 Task Complexity Stress-Test ‣ Appendix D Additional Analyses ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, and for quality and termination rate on Table <a href="#A4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ D.1 Task Complexity Stress-Test ‣ Appendix D Additional Analyses ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<td id="A4.T5.2.1.4.13" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFFFF;padding:0.6pt 2.5pt;"><span id="A4.T5.2.1.4.13.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFFFF;">1</span></td>
<td id="A4.T5.2.1.4.14" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FEFFFE;padding:0.6pt 2.5pt;"><span id="A4.T5.2.1.4.14.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FEFFFE;">1</span></td>

<td id="A4.T6.2.1.14.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="--ltx-bg-color:#DAE8F3;padding:0.6pt 2.5pt;"><span id="A4.T6.2.1.14.8.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#DAE8F3;">80 <span id="A4.T6.2.1.14.8.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">width</span></span></td>
<td id="A4.T6.2.1.14.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="--ltx-bg-color:#CBDFEE;padding:0.6pt 2.5pt;"><span id="A4.T6.2.1.14.9.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#CBDFEE;">98</span></td>

<td id="A4.T6.2.1.14.13" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="--ltx-bg-color:#D8E7F2;padding:0.6pt 2.5pt;"><span id="A4.T6.2.1.14.13.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#D8E7F2;">75</span></td>

</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 6: </span>Quality and Terminated by number of task subgoals (1–7). Both task-fidelity metrics use blue shading. Values are rounded to whole percentages; darker shading indicates higher unrounded scores, with one scale per metric across all seven buckets and simulated models. Human Reference remains unshaded and is treated as terminated by construction.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.2 </span>Training Dynamics</h3>

<div id="A4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Having established the importance of using dynamic discriminators in Section <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Reward Design Alternatives ‣ 4 Results and Analysis ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>, we explore the training dynamics they induce.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.F15" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.31512v1/naturalness_and_jsd_panels.svg" id="A4.F15.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:516/189;" width="516" height="189"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 15: </span>(a) Naturalness reward throughout training for the Fixed Discriminator and LLM Judge - Likert and Winrate ablations; (b) Naturalness reward throughout training for the dynamic discriminator experiments; (c) Average of the Jensen-Shannon Divergence between utterance-length histograms and turn-count histograms for model-generated and real validation conversations. Lower is better.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Models learn to fool each preceding discriminator, while retrained discriminators can detect simulated rollouts from preceding steps.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze the performance of each trained discriminator on each validation step. We run inference on each validation step’s simulated rollouts using the trained discriminators. Figure <a href="#A4.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ Dynamic discriminators help maintain alignment with human reference distributions. ‣ D.2 Training Dynamics ‣ Appendix D Additional Analyses ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a> contains results for UserLM-2.0. The rows represent validation steps, while columns represent the discriminator used to evaluate them. Each index then contains the average <math id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{disc}}(y=\text{real}\mid\hat{u_{1}}...\hat{u_{k}},c)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>disc</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>real</mtext></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{disc}}(y=\text{real}\mid\hat{u_{1}}...\hat{u_{k}},c)</annotation></semantics></math> for the corresponding validation step rollouts using the corresponding discriminator.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For UserLM-2.0, the matrices have a triangular structure. The lower triangular component, featuring validation steps evaluated by earlier discriminators, each predominantly have high <math id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{disc}}(y=\text{real})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>disc</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>real</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{disc}}(y=\text{real})</annotation></semantics></math> values for simulated rollouts. This indicates that as models learn to fool a newly retrained discriminator, they also keep on fooling earlier discriminators. Simultaneously, the upper triangular component predominantly features low <math id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{disc}}(y=\text{real})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>disc</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>real</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{disc}}(y=\text{real})</annotation></semantics></math> values. This is intuitive, as each retrained discriminator is trained on both the most recent 25 steps and simulated conversations from earlier in training. This enables retrained discriminators to remain robust to and discourage reward hacking behavior from early steps as well.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Dynamic discriminators help maintain alignment with human reference distributions.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To better understand how dynamic discriminators then affect alignment with the human reference distribution, we look at output-length and conversation turn-counts as proxies. Specifically, we construct histograms of output-length and turn-counts for all models, using their validation rollouts during training, and compare them against histograms for corresponding human interactions using Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD). Figure <a href="#A4.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ D.2 Training Dynamics ‣ Appendix D Additional Analyses ‣ Towards User Simulators That Stay on Task and Still Sound Natural" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>(c) plots the averaged JSD value over training. Both the UserLM-2.0 and No Coverage runs sustain a low JSD throughout training and can correct themselves when JSD spikes. The alternative reward variants and the No Naturalness ablation, on the other hand, each increasingly diverges. This divergence is driven primarily by an increase in output-length, with the LLM judge variants ultimately reaching up to 400 words per turn on average.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.F16" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.31512v1/mean_prob_real_simulated.png" id="A4.F16.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:574/355;" width="574" height="355" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 16: </span>For UserLM-2.0, we perform inference with each discriminator trained during RL on validation rollouts from each validation step and report <math id="A4.F16.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{disc}}(y=\text{real}\mid\hat{u_{1}}...\hat{u_{k}},c)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>disc</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>real</mtext></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{disc}}(y=\text{real}\mid\hat{u_{1}}...\hat{u_{k}},c)</annotation></semantics></math> for generated conversations. Blue and red indicate high and low probabilities respectively. UserLM-2.0 learns not only to fool the most recent discriminator, but also keeps fooling older ones as well.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
</article>
